content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published consolidated guidelines on the management of tuberculosis (TB) in children and adolescents, titled Module 5: Management of Tuberculosis in Children and Adolescents. These guidelines are available in both electronic and print versions, with respective ISBNs 978-92-4-004676-4 and 978-92-4-004677-1. The guidelines include recommendations on TB screening, prevention, diagnostics, treatment, and care models specific to children and adolescents. They also address special situations and research priorities. The document emphasizes that the designations and presentation of material do not imply any opinion on the legal status of countries, territories, or boundaries. WHO has taken precautions to verify the information but provides it without warranty, and the responsibility for its interpretation and use lies with the reader. The development of these guidelines was coordinated by Sabine Verkuijl, Annemieke Brands, Kerri Viney, and Tiziana Masini, under the guidance of Farai Mavhunga and the overall direction of Tereza Kasaeva, Director of the WHO Global TB Programme. Contributions were made by colleagues from the Prevention, Diagnosis, Treatment, Care, and Innovation Unit of the Global TB Programme, led by Matteo Zignol. External reviewers and experts from various institutions worldwide also provided input, ensuring a comprehensive and evidence-based approach. The guidelines address specific PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) questions related to TB management in children and adolescents. These include topics such as TB screening, diagnostic algorithms, the use of Xpert Ultra for pulmonary TB diagnosis, treatment shortening for non-severe drug-susceptible TB, the use of bedaquiline and delamanid in younger children with multidrug-resistant TB, and the treatment of TB meningitis. Additionally, the guidelines explore models of care for TB case detection and prevention in high-burden settings, as well as the socioeconomic impact of TB on affected families and strategies for engaging adolescents in their care. The production of the guidelines involved a wide range of contributors, including clinicians, researchers, and public health experts from institutions across the globe. Their expertise ensured that the recommendations are grounded in the latest scientific evidence and tailored to the unique needs of children and adolescents affected by TB.
